title: Representing Noise in Circuits
intro: Output noise is what you measure, but it scales with gain, so circuits are compared by their input-referred noise. In general that takes two sources, a series voltage and a parallel current, and they are usually correlated.

blocks.text: Zero the input, find each source's contribution at the output and add. For a CS stage with resistive load ($\lambda = 0$), the transistor's thermal and flicker currents and the load's current all flow into $R_D$:

Adding a noiseless gain stage after the CS stage multiplies the output noise but not the SNR, so output noise alone is a misleading figure of merit. Instead place one source $\overline{V_{n,in}^2}$ at the input of a noiseless copy so that it produces the same output: divide by $A_v^2$. For the CS stage

The first term is the thermal noise of a resistor $\gamma/g_m$ in series with the gate; the last is a resistor $1/(g_m^2R_D)$. The total thermal part is often quoted as an equivalent noise resistance $R_T$ with $\overline{V_{n,in}^2} = 4kTR_T$. The load's share falls as $R_D$ rises, because its output noise grows as $\sqrt{R_D}$ while the gain grows as $R_D$. Input-referred noise cannot be measured at the input; it is a fiction that tells you how small a signal the circuit can detect.
Why a current source is also needed

Give the CS stage an input capacitance $C_{in}$ and drive it from a source resistance $R_1$. With only a voltage source at the input, $R_1$ and $C_{in}$ would filter it, and the output noise would vanish as $R_1 \to \infty$. But the transistor's noise reaches the output whatever drives the gate. The fix is a second source, a current $\overline{I_{n,in}^2}$ in parallel with the input; together the two represent any linear two-port exactly.

blocks.alt: A source with impedance ZS drives a series noise voltage source Vn,in squared, then a node with a noise current source In,in squared to ground, then a noiseless copy of the circuit.
blocks.caption: The general input-referred model.

items: Input shorted ($Z_S = 0$): the current source is bypassed; equate output noises to get $\overline{V_{n,in}^2}$.
Input open ($Z_S \to \infty$): the voltage source carries no current; equate output noises to get $\overline{I_{n,in}^2}$.

blocks.text: For the CS stage with $C_{in}$ (thermal noise only), the open-input output noise $4kT(\gamma g_m + 1/R_D)R_D^2$ must equal $\overline{I_{n,in}^2}(1/C_{in}\omega)^2g_m^2R_D^2$:

At a node X fed from an impedance $Z_S$, the total noise is $V_{n,X} = \frac{Z_{in}}{Z_{in} + Z_S}V_{n,in} + \frac{Z_{in}Z_S}{Z_{in} + Z_S}I_{n,in}$. The current source can be ignored when the driving impedance is small enough, whatever $Z_{in}$ is:
Correlation, and why nothing is counted twice

$V_{n,in}$ and $I_{n,in}$ often come from the same physical sources, so they are correlated and must be added as voltages, not powers. For the CS stage, $V_{n,in} = V_{n,M1} + V_{n,RD}/(g_mR_D)$ and $I_{n,in} = C_{in}s\,V_{n,in}$. Substituting into the node-X expression gives $V_{n,X} = V_{n,M1} + V_{n,RD}/(g_mR_D)$, independent of $Z_S$ and $C_{in}$: the output noise is right for any source, with no double counting.

This is a common case: if the output noise is the same with the input shorted or open, then $I_{n,in} = V_{n,in}/Z_{in}$ (fully correlated), and for any source impedance the input node simply sees $V_{n,X} = V_{n,in}$. Then use the voltage source alone, applied directly at the input node (Razavi, Section 7.10).

Sometimes it is easier to short the output and find the noise current, then divide by a transconductance (input shorted) or a current gain (input open). Example: a transistor with a feedback resistor $R_F$ from drain to gate and an ideal current-source load ($\lambda = 0$).

items: Input and output both shorted: $\overline{I_{n,out}^2} = 4kT/R_F + 4kT\gamma g_m$. The short-circuit transconductance is $G_m = g_m - 1/R_F$, so $\overline{V_{n,in}^2} = \frac{4kT/R_F + 4kT\gamma g_m}{(g_m - 1/R_F)^2}$.

Input open, output shorted: $R_F$'s noise drives the gate directly, giving $\overline{I_{n,out}^2} = 4kTR_Fg_m^2 + 4kT\gamma g_m$. The current gain is $g_mR_F - 1$, so $\overline{I_{n,in}^2} = \frac{4kTR_Fg_m^2 + 4kT\gamma g_m}{(g_mR_F - 1)^2}$.

blocks.text: Here the output noise differs between open and shorted inputs, so both sources matter.

blocks.title: Equivalent noise resistance
blocks.text: A CS stage has $g_m = 5\text{ mS}$, $R_D = 2\text{ k}\Omega$, $\gamma = 1$. Find $R_T$ and the input noise density at 300 K (thermal only).

blocks.title: When does the noise current matter?
blocks.text: The same stage has $C_{in} = 200\text{ fF}$. At 100 MHz find $I_{n,in}$ and the source impedance above which it matters.
solution: $V_{n,in}/I_{n,in} = 1.91\text{ nV}/0.24\text{ pA} \approx 8\text{ k}\Omega$; this equals $1/(C_{in}\omega)$, as the full correlation predicts.
blocks.answer: $0.24\text{ pA}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$; it matters for $|Z_S|$ approaching 8 k$\Omega$.
